title: int(" 42 ") and int("1_000") both just work
assumption: int() only accepts exactly what you could type as an integer literal in source code, with nothing extra around it.

input.description: Converting a number pulled from a config file, environment variable, or user-pasted value that has incidental surrounding whitespace, or a number formatted with underscore thousands-separators (a format Python itself started allowing in source literals in 3.6).

what_goes_wrong: A validation routine that assumes `int()` will reject anything that isn't a bare run of digits lets through both leading/trailing whitespace and underscore-separated digit groups, silently accepting input shapes the developer never intended to allow.
why: `int()`'s string-to-integer conversion strips leading and trailing whitespace before parsing, by design, and that means any Unicode whitespace (tabs, newlines, U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE), not just spaces. Separately, since Python 3.6 (PEP 515), the integer literal grammar allows a single underscore between digits as a visual separator (`1_000`), and `int()`'s string parsing follows that same grammar, so it accepts underscore-separated digit strings too -- as long as the underscores are singly placed between digits, not leading, trailing, or doubled.

repros.expected_output:
42
1000
leading underscore rejected: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '_1000'

fix: Don't assume `int()` validates format as strictly as a literal; if you need to reject whitespace or separators, check the string's shape explicitly (e.g. a regex) before calling `int()`.
